title: Near-patient diagnosis of the cause and treatability of most serious infections

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an affordable diagnostic capability available close to where a patient receives care that answers three connected questions: what is causing a serious infection, whether a detected organism actually explains the illness, and which available treatments are likely to work. It would deliver results quickly enough to guide initial treatment across diverse infection syndromes and specimen types, including mixed infections and organisms that were not anticipated when the test was designed. This is a proposed capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

Conceptual synthesis: the advance requires an integrated chain of detection, causal interpretation and actionable susceptibility assessment, with uncertainty communicated at each stage. Detecting microbial genetic material would not by itself establish the cause of illness or determine effective treatment. A faster assay restricted to a fixed list of organisms could contribute to this capability, but would cover only part of its intended breadth. “Most serious infections” describes an ambition whose clinical coverage still needs an operational definition.

significance.text: Conditional significance: if the proposed accuracy, speed, affordability and breadth were demonstrated, clinicians could make informed treatment decisions at the first encounter across many serious infections. The direct advance would be timely, actionable diagnostic information. Reduced reliance on empiric treatment would be a potential consequence whose extent depends on specimen availability, diagnostic reliability and whether results arrive before treatment decisions must be made.

Further potential benefits include more appropriate use of existing antimicrobials and earlier recognition of infections outside familiar diagnostic panels. These possibilities require clinical demonstration. Identifying an unfamiliar organism is useful only when there is enough evidence to interpret its relevance to the patient, and a susceptibility result helps only when it can inform an available treatment. Faster laboratory information alone does not establish improved patient outcomes.

An important limit is that this would improve diagnosis and treatment selection; it would not itself create a drug for an untreatable infection, prevent transmission or replace vaccination. Its revolutionary scope therefore rests on combining breadth, accessibility and clinical interpretation, rather than speed alone. These are implications of the proposed concept, not measured effects established by the supplied sources.

missing_breakthrough.text: Conceptual barrier: a broadly useful near-patient system must obtain a clinically meaningful answer from specimens that may contain very little relevant microbial material—or none from the actual site of infection. Greater analytical sensitivity cannot recover a pathogen that is absent from the collected specimen. The proposed capability therefore requires suitable sampling strategies and explicit recognition of when a negative result cannot safely exclude infection. The supplied scientific artifacts do not independently substantiate the frequency or magnitude of these limitations.

Conceptual barrier: detection must be connected to causation. Contamination, harmless colonization and multiple detected organisms can complicate attribution of illness. The system would need to distinguish plausible causes from incidental findings, recognize mixed infections and communicate unresolved alternatives. For previously unrecognized organisms, discovering a sequence and establishing clinical relevance are separate tasks.

Conceptual barrier: pathogen identification must also be connected to treatment response. The research raises the limitation that a genome alone may not reliably predict drug response; the supplied evidence does not establish when or how often this occurs. The missing capability is therefore actionable susceptibility assessment with a defined scope and uncertainty, rather than an assumption that identifying genetic material completes the treatment decision.

Engineering synthesis: these functions must work together within the time, cost, staffing and infrastructure constraints of hospitals and resource-limited clinics. A convincing system must preserve diagnostic and susceptibility performance while moving testing close to care. A successful individual component would be partial progress; the proposed innovation requires the combined workflow to remain clinically useful.

current_state.text: The research identifies clinical metagenomic sequencing as an existing approach to broad organism detection and names a study attributed to Benoit and colleagues, “Seven-year performance of a clinical metagenomic next-generation sequencing test for diagnosis of central nervous system infections,” with a reported publication date of 12 November 2024. It reports 63.1% sensitivity in an evaluated subset and missed infections where microbial material was absent from cerebrospinal fluid. Those details remain unverified in the supplied review: the retained PubMed material contains a cookie-access message rather than article content, and the earlier inspection on which the research relies was not supplied. The denominator, reference standard and precise meaning of the reported sensitivity therefore cannot be established here, and the number should not be generalized to other specimens or serious infections.

The research also names a study attributed to Banerjee and colleagues, “Fast Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing for Gram-Negative Bacteremia: The FAST Randomized Clinical Trial,” with a reported publication date of 18 April 2026. It describes rapid testing as failing to show superiority on the overall trial outcome. No article text was retained for the supplied JAMA link, so the study identity, date, endpoint and result cannot be independently confirmed from these inputs. The reported conclusion must remain an unverified account; it cannot establish either clinical benefit or absence of benefit. The broader distinction remains useful: faster susceptibility results and improved clinical outcomes are separate propositions.

Evidence boundary: the supplied materials do not establish a demonstrated system that combines broad detection, causal interpretation, actionable susceptibility and near-patient accessibility across most serious infections. They also do not provide a substantive search record supporting an assessment of developments through 1 November 2026. This limits what can be concluded about current achievements and whether the full capability remains unsolved; it is not evidence that the referenced studies are false or that no further progress exists.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: prospective studies should evaluate the integrated workflow in hospitals and resource-limited clinics across prespecified serious-infection syndromes, patient populations and specimen types. Coverage should include mixed infections and organisms outside the system’s anticipated targets, with clear definitions of what counts as previously unrecognized. The studies should define the clinical denominator behind “most serious infections.” Finite evaluations would establish demonstrated breadth within their tested settings, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Prospective integrated workflow studies establish breadth across serious infections

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement framework: before evaluation, investigators should specify acceptable turnaround time from sampling to an actionable result, affordability, diagnostic accuracy, causal-attribution performance and susceptibility performance. They should separately assess pathogen detection, interpretation of clinical relevance and treatment guidance. Uncertainty reporting should be evaluated explicitly, including how the system handles inadequate specimens, ambiguous detections, incomplete susceptibility coverage and negative results that cannot exclude infection. These are proposed criteria, not established standards, and no numerical thresholds are supplied.
completion_criteria.label: Prespecified diagnostic performance criteria include explicit uncertainty assessment

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: randomized implementation studies should show improved patient outcomes or more appropriate treatment, using clearly defined endpoints and prespecified acceptable rates of dangerous false reassurance and false attribution. Evaluation should establish whether results arrive in time to change decisions, whether clinicians act on them appropriately and whether recommended treatments are available. Faster analytical results alone would not satisfy the clinical-benefit claim.
completion_criteria.label: Randomized implementation studies demonstrate clinical benefit within prespecified safety limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent sites should reproduce performance across operators, routine specimen handling and the infrastructure conditions of intended use. Reports should identify excluded syndromes and specimens, failure rates, costs and circumstances requiring additional testing or specialist interpretation. Demonstrated success could support a bounded clinical claim while preserving explicit limitations outside the evaluated scope.
completion_criteria.label: Independent sites reproduce routine performance and report practical limitations

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: INF-06, a dependable platform for generating new antibacterial treatments, and INF-15, a rapidly adaptable clinical phage-therapy platform, overlap most directly through treatment selection. INF-05 could help identify relevant infections and assess susceptibility, while those concepts concern producing or adapting therapies. INF-07, broad-spectrum treatment for unrelated viral infections, could reduce some dependence on identifying a specific virus before treatment, but would not answer all questions of causation, coverage or treatability.

Roster-based synthesis: INF-02, a safe, scalable cure for established HIV infection; INF-11, a safe, broadly effective treatment-free cure for chronic hepatitis B; and INF-12, very short, reliable curative treatment for active and latent tuberculosis, concern achieving durable therapeutic outcomes. INF-05 could support diagnosis or treatment decisions where applicable, but identifying an infection and its likely drug response does not establish a cure or demonstrate eradication of persistent infection.

Roster-based synthesis: INF-01, a broadly protective HIV vaccine; INF-03, a tuberculosis vaccine that interrupts transmission; INF-08, a pre-emptive vaccine against diverse pandemic coronaviruses; and INF-13, a highly protective, durable and readily deliverable malaria vaccine, concern prevention. INF-04, a reliable way to break malaria transmission through its vectors, concerns interruption of transmission. INF-05 addresses diagnosis during clinical care and could complement these approaches, while remaining a distinct capability.

Roster-based synthesis: INF-09, a rapid, end-to-end vaccine response to a newly identified pathogen, shares the need to recognize unfamiliar infectious threats. Near-patient detection could potentially contribute early clinical information, but vaccine development and deployment require a separate response capability. INF-10, prevention of multiple sclerosis by controlling Epstein–Barr virus, and INF-14, mechanism-guided prevention of major post-viral syndromes, share questions about linking infection to disease. Detecting an organism during an acute illness would not by itself establish its causal role in a later condition or demonstrate that controlling it prevents that condition.

change_log.change: Preserved INF-05 and its title while expanding the explanation of the integrated diagnostic capability.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent despite limitations in the supporting evidence; detection, causal interpretation and susceptibility are distinct requirements.

change_log.change: Made reductions in empiric treatment and improvements in outcomes conditional.
change_log.reason: Their extent depends on diagnostic coverage, specimen adequacy, timing, treatment availability and clinical implementation.

change_log.change: Retained the reported 63.1% sensitivity and cerebrospinal-fluid sampling finding as explicitly unverified accounts.
change_log.reason: The retained PubMed artifact contains no scientific article content, and the referenced first-pass inspection is unavailable.

change_log.change: Qualified the FAST trial attribution, date and reported lack of superiority.
change_log.reason: No retained trial text permits confirmation of its identity, endpoint or result; missing evidence cannot establish a negative clinical finding.

change_log.change: Integrated the sampling, causation and genotype-to-treatment distinctions into the relevant scientific barriers.
change_log.reason: These distinctions explain why broad organism detection alone would not complete the proposed capability, while their empirical basis remains unverified here.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria to include prespecified thresholds, susceptibility, uncertainty, independent reproducibility and practical boundaries.
change_log.reason: These additions make the ambition assessable without inventing numerical standards or implying finite testing establishes universality.

change_log.change: Explained relationships with every other supplied roster entry without merging concepts.
change_log.reason: Diagnostic information can complement prevention and therapy while remaining distinct from achieving those interventions.

unresolved_issues: The underlying scientific basis for the stated diagnostic barriers is not independently documented by substantive source content in the supplied materials.
The reported metagenomic study identity, publication date, 63.1% sensitivity, evaluated subset, reference standard and sampling-related missed infections require confirmation from article content.
The FAST trial identity, publication date, primary endpoint, effect estimates and reported lack of superiority remain unverified.
The supplied search record cannot establish developments through 1 November 2026 or resolve whether the full proposed capability remains open.
“Near-patient,” “rapid,” “affordable,” “most serious infections” and acceptable error rates need operational definitions; the inputs supply no numerical thresholds.
The intended treatment classes and scope of actionable susceptibility assessment remain unspecified.
No substantive review recommendation was rejected; recommendations requiring scientific verification remain unresolved because new research was excluded.

brief.title: Finding infection causes and effective treatments nearby
possible: At a hospital or local clinic, someone with a serious infection could get an affordable answer in time to guide their first treatment: what is causing the illness and which available medicines are likely to work.

The same service could handle many kinds of serious infection, including infections caused by several organisms together or by organisms the test’s designers did not anticipate. It could distinguish a cause of illness from a harmless organism found in the sample.
why: Clinicians could choose treatment with less guesswork at the first encounter. Patients could receive more appropriate medicines, and unfamiliar infections could be recognized earlier.

sources.who: Patrick Benoit and colleagues, University of California, San Francisco
sources.showed: A laboratory test that reads genetic material from many kinds of microbes identified infections of the brain and spinal cord. It found some infections that other tests missed.
sources.quote: When only considering diagnoses made by CSF direct detection testing, the sensitivity of mNGS testing increased to 86%.
sources.cited_for: Broad testing of fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord can find causes missed by other diagnostic tests.
sources.not_established: The study did not establish a nearby, affordable service that also selects effective treatments across most serious infections.

sources.showed: This is a randomized clinical trial of rapid testing to determine which medicines work against certain bacteria causing bloodstream infections.
sources.cited_for: The trial addresses whether faster drug-response testing improves clinical care.
sources.not_established: Faster drug-response results alone do not establish better patient outcomes.

shown: Benoit and colleagues evaluated broad genetic testing for infections of the brain and spinal cord. In the clinically assessed subset, it detected 63.1% of infections. Some diagnoses came from this test alone, but results typically took days.
missing: Sampling must yield useful answers even when little microbial material is present, while identifying negative results that cannot rule out infection.
A combined test must distinguish illness-causing organisms from contamination or harmless organisms, including when several organisms appear.
Organism detection must connect reliably to which available medicines will work, with clear limits on treatment guidance.
The complete service must work quickly and affordably near patients across diverse serious infections, including in clinics with limited resources.

milestones.label: Broad coverage demonstrated in real patient care
milestones.explanation: Studies following patients through care would have to demonstrate the complete service across defined illnesses, samples and settings, including mixed and unexpected infections. This would establish its clinical reach.

milestones.label: Performance and uncertainty meet criteria set before testing
milestones.explanation: Evaluation would have to assess speed, cost, detection, cause identification, treatment guidance and uncertainty against criteria set beforehand. This would establish when clinicians can rely on the answers.

milestones.label: Randomized studies demonstrate clinical benefit within safety limits
milestones.explanation: Studies randomly assigning use of the service would have to show better outcomes or treatment within preset limits on dangerous errors. This would establish whether timely results improve care.

milestones.label: Independent sites reproduce results in routine use
milestones.explanation: Independent sites would have to reproduce performance under everyday conditions and report failures, costs and situations needing further testing. This would establish practical reliability and limits.

uncertain: What share of serious infections would count as sufficient coverage, and what speed, cost and error rates would be acceptable?
Which treatments could the service assess reliably, especially when an organism’s genetic material does not settle how it responds to drugs?

page.title: Near-patient pathogen identification and susceptibility testing
page.definition: A service at the site of care identifies which organisms are causing a serious infection and reports which drugs are active against them in time to guide treatment. It distinguishes infection from incidental detection across clinical syndromes, including infections with several organisms and pathogens outside preset panels. A laboratory sequencing test for complicated urinary tract infection illustrates part of this capability: it identifies organisms in urine and predicts their susceptibility in about four hours from laboratory receipt.

goal.need: At 131 US hospitals, 4,165 of 21,608 patients treated on the day of their first blood culture received no antibiotic active against their bloodstream isolate. Urine culture and susceptibility results can take two to four days. Earlier results can help clinicians replace an inactive drug or narrow treatment. A test for selected resistance genes can leave that choice unresolved. In gram-negative bloodstream infection, rapid testing brought antibiotic changes forward by a median of 14 hours without a demonstrated improvement in 30-day outcomes.

completion.title: Independent clinical evaluation reproduces an integrated near-patient diagnostic service’s claims.
completion.criterion: Independent prospective evaluations reproduce an integrated near-patient service’s registered clinical claims: causal pathogen attribution, actionable susceptibility, results before the treatment decision, and operation within intended-site cost and infrastructure limits. Claims are validated against clinical adjudication and reference susceptibility methods, with patient benefit established in randomised comparisons. Validation spans prespecified serious-infection syndromes and includes mixed infections and organisms outside preset panels; coverage uses all eligible patients as its denominator.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; proposed integrated clinical-demonstration test.
completion.basis: Searches of WHO diagnostic priorities, ICMR sepsis product profiles, NIH/BARDA prize criteria and DARPA’s DIGET goals found no joint threshold for coverage, causation, susceptibility, turnaround and cost. The Atlas proposes independent reproduction of an integrated clinical demonstration. No published denominator or numerical coverage threshold supports certifying “most serious infections”; achievement therefore applies only to the validated clinical scope.

milestones.title: A susceptibility assay reaches ≥90% essential and categorical agreement in gram-negative blood cultures.
milestones.criterion: For positive blood cultures containing gram-negative rods, compare results with reference broth microdilution under K230675. Essential agreement requires minimum inhibitory concentrations within one twofold dilution of the reference. Categorical agreement requires the same susceptibility category. Both agreement rates must be ≥90%, false resistance ≤3% of reference-susceptible results and false susceptibility ≤2% of reference-resistant results, subject to the decision’s specified adjustments and organism–drug exceptions.
milestones.set_by: US FDA; K230675 decision summary, page 26. Written for gram-negative positive blood cultures.
milestones.threshold_quote: Performance was considered acceptable if the EA and CA were ≥90%, major error rate was ≤3%, and very major error rate was ≤2%.

milestones.title: A sepsis blood test identifies 90% of bacterial isolates to species and 95% to genus.
milestones.criterion: Using 1 mL of venous blood and blood culture as the reference, meet the TPP.S.II minimal diagnostic sensitivity target of 85–90% and identify 90% of isolates to species and 95% to genus. The minimal panel covers Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus spp., Staphylococcus aureus, Enterococcus spp., Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Salmonella.
milestones.set_by: ICMR task force and Technical Advisory Group on AMR Diagnostics, Supplementary Table II, TPP.S.II, minimal targets.
milestones.threshold_quote: Identifies 90 per cent of isolates to species level, 95 per cent to genus level

milestones.title: An antimicrobial susceptibility assay receives FDA 510(k) clearance for its labelled use.
milestones.criterion: FDA issues a 510(k) decision finding the susceptibility assay substantially equivalent for its labelled clinical use. The decision applies to the specimen types, organisms and conditions in the cleared indication.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 510(k) Premarket Notification database and decision summary.

milestones.title: Near-patient tests identify pathogens within 4 hours and return susceptibility results in under 4 hours.
milestones.criterion: Achieve ICMR TPP.S.II/III’s optimal turnaround, handling, reproducibility and price targets at district or sub-district hospitals: identification ≤4 h; susceptibility profiling <4 h; each with ≤500 µL input, <10 min hands-on time and κ≥0.9 inter-user/site reproducibility. Individual-test prices are ≤INR 500 and ≤INR 2000, respectively. Related urine evidence, published on 3 December 2025, used 53 samples from a 78-patient complicated-UTI cohort: sequencing gave 589/653 susceptibility predictions concordant with VITEK-2 in approximately 4 h from laboratory receipt. This was not a sepsis deployment test.
milestones.set_by: ICMR task force and Technical Advisory Group on AMR Diagnostics; Supplementary Table II, TPP.S.II/III, optimal operational targets for sepsis. Thresholds appear only in the tables.

milestones.title: Rapid testing yields a better 30-day outcome with a lower 95% probability bound above 50%.
milestones.criterion: In hospitalized patients with gram-negative bloodstream infection, randomize rapid phenotypic susceptibility testing plus standard testing against standard testing alone, with antimicrobial stewardship review in both groups. Rank 30-day outcomes from best to worst as alive without a deleterious event, alive with at least one such event, and death. Count a tie as one-half. The lower 95% confidence limit for the probability of a better outcome with rapid testing must exceed 50%.
milestones.set_by: Antibacterial Resistance Leadership Group; FAST protocol NCT06174649 and its published superiority criterion. This test was written for gram-negative bloodstream infection.
milestones.threshold_quote: Superiority was concluded if the lower limit of the 95% CI exceeded 50%.

milestones.title: An integrated near-patient service meets registered diagnostic and treatment endpoints in clinical use.
milestones.criterion: In a first prospective evaluation at the intended care sites, meet the diagnostic, treatment-selection and patient-outcome endpoints registered before enrolment. Evaluate the complete service across the prespecified syndromes, including mixed infections and organisms outside preset panels. Compare causal attribution with clinical adjudication and susceptibility with reference testing. Assess whether results reach clinicians before the treatment decision, whether site cost and infrastructure limits are met, and whether patients benefit in a randomized comparison. Report coverage among all eligible patients.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas proposes this integration milestone. No external body identified defines a test for the complete clinical workflow.

milestones.title: A diagnostic prototype demonstrates analytical performance on clinical or contrived specimens.
milestones.criterion: Operate the point-of-care diagnostic prototype on clinical or contrived specimens and report data supporting its analytical performance claims for the intended specimen type. Both a working device and data from its use are required.
milestones.set_by: NIH and BARDA, Antimicrobial Resistance Diagnostic Challenge, Step 2.
milestones.threshold_quote: actual use of the device in testing contrived or clinical specimens

milestones.title: Two independent certified laboratories confirm a diagnostic prototype’s analytical claims.
milestones.criterion: Two independent laboratories certified under the US Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments compare the prototype with standard FDA-approved assays using characterized pathogens, clinical specimens or contrived samples. They assess usability, stated time to result, analytical sensitivity and specificity, and confirm the analytical performance reported for the prototype in Step 2.
milestones.set_by: NIH and BARDA, Antimicrobial Resistance Diagnostic Challenge, Step 3.
milestones.threshold_quote: Each solution will be tested by two CLIA-certified laboratories against standard FDA-approved in vitro assays

milestones.title: A district-hospital platform identifies priority bacteria and reports phenotypic susceptibility in 2–3 h.
milestones.criterion: Meet the optimal turnaround target in WHO Annex I, characteristic 41, for both bacterial identification and phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility on the multiplex platform at a district hospital or higher-level facility. The minimal target is a same-day result and the optimal target is 2–3 hours. WHO assigns a separate turnaround target to identification paired with genotypic resistance testing.
milestones.set_by: World Health Organization, Target product profiles for antibacterial resistance diagnostics, Annex I, characteristic 41.

milestones.title: A sepsis test identifies blood pathogens within 4 hours at a price of ≤INR 500 per test.
milestones.criterion: At a sub-district hospital or higher level, identify pathogens from ≤500 µL of venous blood in ≤4 hours with <10 minutes of hands-on time. The individual test price is ≤INR 500 and agreement between users and testing sites reaches κ≥0.9.
milestones.set_by: ICMR task force and Technical Advisory Group on AMR Diagnostics, Supplementary Table II, TPP.S.II, optimal identification targets.

milestones.title: A sepsis test reports antimicrobial susceptibility in under 4 hours at ≤INR 2,000 per test.
milestones.criterion: At a sub-district hospital or higher level, report pathogen-specific susceptibility or resistance from ≤500 µL of whole blood in <4 hours with <10 minutes of hands-on time. The individual test price is ≤INR 2,000 and agreement between users and testing sites reaches κ≥0.9. TPP.S.III specifies CLSI or EUCAST reference standards.
milestones.set_by: ICMR task force and Technical Advisory Group on AMR Diagnostics, Supplementary Table II, TPP.S.III, optimal susceptibility-profiling targets.

not_found: Searches of WHO, ICMR, NIH/BARDA and DARPA documents found no external definition of the proportion or denominator meant by “most serious infections”.
No joint published acceptance test for causal attribution, susceptibility, speed, affordability and breadth across serious infections was located.
No demonstration meeting the complete integrated capability, including mixed infections and organisms outside preset panels, was located.
No study reporting all the cited ICMR sepsis performance and deployment targets together was located.

results.finding: For 1,130 UCSF CSF samples, median mNGS laboratory turnaround was 3.6 days.
results.detail: The laboratory turnaround exceeded the four-hour identification target. The study evaluated a centralized identification assay, not the complete near-patient identification and susceptibility workflow.
results.quote:
The median turnaround times for UCSF and non-UCSF patients were 8.2 and 11.4 days, respectively, from sample collection to result (P
< 0.0001), and 3.6 and 3.8 days, respectively, from start of sample processing in the laboratory to result (P
< 0.0001).

results.finding: Among 670 positive blood cultures, the assay returned susceptibility reports in under 2 hours.
results.detail: Timing began after blood cultures became positive; organisms were identified separately. The assay used 1 mL of culture, excluded polymicrobial samples, and was tested in laboratories and university hospitals. Price and κ reproducibility were not reported.
results.quote: A proprietary software (bioFAST) was used to immediately generate a susceptibility report in less than 2 h.

results.finding: In 278 women with suspected uncomplicated UTI, the near-patient PA-100 returned susceptibility results within 45 min.
results.detail: The 400 µL urine input met the volume target, but the device did not report pathogen species. Hands-on time, inter-user/site reproducibility, price and district or sub-district hospital deployment were not reported. Patients with complicated UTI were excluded.
results.quote: The analyser delivered bacteriuria results in 15 min and AST results within 45 min.

results.finding: QolorPhAST identified bacteria and profiled susceptibility in a suspected-UTI cohort of unspecified size in 36 minutes.
results.detail: The text reports 50 urine specimens for a no-antibiotic growth condition but does not specify the size of the identification and susceptibility cohort. It does not establish district-hospital deployment or the required input volume, hands-on time, inter-user/site reproducibility and individual-test prices.
results.quote: In a proof-of-concept clinical study, QolorPhAST was tested with a cohort of blinded patient samples suspected of urinary tract infections, achieving 100% accuracy in species identification, an average categorical agreement of 91.81% and an average essential agreement of 86.4%, with a turnaround time of 36 min from specimen introduction to result.

results.finding: UCSF clinical metagenomic sequencing returned a pathogen-positive result in 14.4% of 4,828 cerebrospinal fluid specimens.
results.detail: The positivity rate is diagnostic yield in the tested population. The paper cites prior analytical validation for the assay.
results.quote: After excluding microorganisms reported as contaminants, 697 (14.4%) of 4,828 samples were positive for detection of a pathogen

results.finding: Cerebrospinal fluid metagenomic sequencing had 63.1% sensitivity for CNS infection in a retrospective cohort of 1,164 samples.
results.detail: The composite diagnosis incorporated sequencing results. Among 135 true-positive results, median time from specimen collection to result was nine days.
results.quote: The sensitivity, specificity and accuracy of mNGS testing for CNS infections were 63.1%, 99.6% and 92.9%, respectively.

results.finding: VITEK REVEAL tested 82 gram-negative isolates in contrived positive blood cultures, with ≥95% best-case MIC reproducibility per antimicrobial.
results.detail: Reproducibility used the device’s modal MIC as the comparator. Best-case analysis assumed off-scale results were less than one dilution from that mode.
results.quote:
The best-case reproducibility for each antimicrobial was ≥ 95%, which is 
acceptable.

results.finding: VITEK REVEAL achieved 90.8% categorical agreement for amoxicillin/clavulanate in 500 Enterobacterales blood culture specimens.
results.detail: The decision accepts some low categorical agreement driven by minor errors, adjusts certain errors within one dilution for agents without an intermediate category, and requires alternate testing for specified organism–drug results.
results.quote:
The results from 
clinical and challenge testing demonstrated an EA of 95% and CA of 90.8%. There were 43 
minor (8.6%), 3 major (0.7%) and no very major errors.

results.finding: VITEK REVEAL testing of 82 gram-negative isolates showed ≥89% worst-case MIC reproducibility across three sites.
results.detail: The reproducibility comparison used the device’s modal MIC. FDA-cleared identification methods supplied organism inputs for the susceptibility study.
results.quote: Worst-case reproducibility was ≥ 89% for all antibiotics, which is acceptable.

results.finding: FDA cleared VITEK REVEAL GN AST under K230675 for its labeled positive blood culture use, supported by 1,115 cultures.
results.detail: The indication requires separate organism identification for susceptibility interpretation and reporting.
results.quote:
510(k) SUBSTANTIAL EQUIVALENCE DETERMINATION 
DECISION SUMMARY 
ASSAY AND INSTRUMENT

results.finding: PhenEXA achieved 97.8% categorical agreement with broth microdilution across 23 culture-positive urine specimens.
results.detail: The pilot used a research-laboratory workflow in which urine aliquots were incubated, frozen, and thawed before on-chip susceptibility readout.
results.quote: In a pilot study of 33 patients with suspected UTIs, it achieved 100% species ID accuracy and 97.8% agreement with standard clinical methods, demonstrating strong potential for clinical use.

results.finding: PhenEXA reported a 51-minute combined identification and phenotypic susceptibility assay time alongside a 33-specimen urine pilot.
results.detail: The reported time describes the parallel assay workflow. The clinical pilot included frozen storage before on-chip susceptibility readout.
results.quote: IDing is performed in parallel with the phenotypic AST workflow; therefore, the combined testing time is determined by the longer AST process, resulting in a total testing time of 51 min.

results.finding: Commercial T2Bacteria Panel, ≥20 spiked whole-blood replicates per strain across 10 strains, had detection limits of 2–11 CFU/mL.
results.detail: The paper's own analytical results are for the FDA-cleared commercial version.
results.quote:
The limits of detection ranged from 2 to
11 CFU/mL ( Appendix Table 2 , available at Annals
.org).

results.finding: T2Bacteria had 90% sensitivity among 39 patients with culture-confirmed bloodstream infection caused by a panel target.
results.detail: Sensitivity was calculated only for infections caused by the five panel targets.
results.quote:
Sensitivity of T2Bacteria for proven BSI was 90%
(95% CI, 76% to 96%) ( Table 2 ).

results.finding: T2Bacteria averaged 3.61 hours to species identification on one-sample loads in a 1,427-patient hospital study.
results.detail: The paper does not state how many runs contributed to each load-specific mean.
results.quote:
Mean time was 3.61 hours (SD, 0.2) for 1 sam-
ple and 7.70 hours (SD, 1.38) for a full load (7 samples).

results.finding: In 1,560 cerebrospinal fluid specimens, the investigational FilmArray ME Panel achieved 100% sensitivity or positive agreement for 9 of 14 targets.
results.detail: Several targets had few comparator-positive specimens. Sensitivity could not be estimated for two targets, and specificity or negative percent agreement was at least 99.2% for every target.
results.quote: The FilmArray ME Panel demonstrated a sensitivity or positive percentage of agreement of 100% for 9 of 14 analytes.

results.finding: In 1,560 cerebrospinal fluid specimens, the FilmArray ME Panel had 99.8% overall target-level agreement with comparator testing.
results.detail: The overall agreement figure includes mostly negative results. The manufacturer designed and funded the study and performed the molecular comparator testing.
results.quote: There were a total of 21,840 individual FilmArray ME analyte tests performed for the 1,560 samples. The overall percentage of agreement between FilmArray and the comparator testing was 99.8% (21,791/21,840).

results.finding: The optimized nanopore workflow achieved 99% pathogen identification accuracy across 53 clinical urine specimens.
results.detail: The workflow used leftover urine specimens in laboratory batches. It missed one Proteus mirabilis detection in a mixed infection.
results.quote: The optimized method (M + BB + NB, method 11) demonstrated an overall accuracy score of 99% (100/101) across 53 samples

results.finding: VITEK REVEAL testing of 9 strains in contrived positive blood cultures achieved >98% agreement for both measures across each bottle type.
results.detail: The assay requires a positive blood culture, confirmation of Gram-negative bacilli by Gram stain, and organism identification from a separate test.
results.quote:
O verall, the average EA and CA for each bottle type across all 
antibiotics tested when compared to the reference MIC was >98% (Table 3)

results.finding: VITEK REVEAL ampicillin/sulbactam testing in 372 Enterobacterales positive blood cultures yielded 77.2% categorical agreement.
results.detail: The summary accepts the ampicillin/sulbactam result based on high evaluable essential agreement and predominantly minor errors. For trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, Table 8 gives 14 false-resistant results among 325 susceptible results (4.3%). The summary gives an E. coli retesting limitation without a recalculated rate.
results.quote:
The overall performance for Enterobacterales species resulted in EA of 97. 8% and CA of 
77.2%.

results.finding: VITEK REVEAL testing at three sites, with 27 results per contrived sample, achieved worst-case reproducibility of ≥91.7% per antimicrobial.
results.detail: The reproducibility comparison used the modal assay result. The separate method-comparison study performed reference broth microdilution at one reference laboratory.
results.quote:
Worst-case reproducibility for each antimicrobial was ≥91.7%, meeting the acceptance 
criteria of ≥89%.

results.finding: FDA cleared the VITEK REVEAL GN AST Assay for labelled use on Gram-negative positive blood cultures under K230675.
results.detail: The finding is one regulatory decision. A specimen sample size does not apply to the clearance itself.
results.quote: have determined the device is substantially equivalent (for the indications for use stated in the enclosure)

results.finding: FASTinov achieved overall sensitivity above 96% across 670 clinical and spiked positive blood cultures.
results.quote: Sensitivity and specificity were >95% for all antimicrobials.

results.finding: FASTgramneg achieved 98.9% EUCAST categorical agreement across 367 gram-negative positive blood cultures.
results.detail: Some drug-level false-susceptibility rates exceeded 2%. For example, ceftolozane–tazobactam had 5 errors among 61 reference-resistant results under EUCAST.

results.finding: Across three sites, FASTgramneg achieved 96.8% EUCAST reproducibility in a comparison using 10 shared spiked cultures.
results.detail: The reproducibility comparison included the developer's laboratory alongside the two hospital laboratories.
results.quote:
Reproducibility regarding FASTgramneg was 96.8%/95% 
and for FASTgrampos was 95.1%/95.1% when using 
EUCAST/CLSI criteria.

results.finding: FASTinov returned phenotypic susceptibility within 117 minutes in a study of 670 positive blood cultures.
results.detail: The measured interval excluded blood culture incubation and MALDI-TOF identification.
results.quote:
TTR had a minimum of 79 min, and maximum of 117 
min, and all tests were performed in less than 2 h.

results.finding: FASTinov returned susceptibility within 117 minutes in a study of 670 positive blood cultures.
results.detail: The reported 5–10 minutes covers sample preparation. The study reports percent reproducibility and gives no kappa estimate.
results.quote:
TTR had a minimum of 79 min, and maximum of 117 
min, and all tests were performed in less than 2 h.

results.finding: PA-100 testing in 278 women with suspected uncomplicated UTI showed 84.0% bacteriuria sensitivity within device specifications.
results.detail: Sensitivity fell to 65.7% (94/143) when the analysis included all microbiologically positive samples regardless of organism or bacterial count.
results.quote:
Under IFU specifica-
tions bacteriuria detection by the PA-100 in positive urine 
cultures was 89 out of 106 (sensitivity 84.0%, CI:75.6% to 
90.4%).

results.finding: In a study of 278 patients with suspected uncomplicated UTI, PA-100 reported phenotypic susceptibility within 45 minutes.
results.detail: The analyser used an internal bacterial grouping to apply susceptibility breakpoints. The user saw the bacteriuria result and susceptibility categories.
results.quote: The analyser delivered bacteriuria results in 15 min and AST results within 45 min.

results.finding: Hypothetical PA-100 recommendations met the culture-based definition of optimal treatment in 78.4% of 278 suspected uncomplicated UTI cases.
results.detail: Optimal treatment meant withholding antibiotics for a negative culture or selecting an active antibiotic for a positive culture. The study excluded complicated UTI and assessed recommendations without changing patient care.
results.quote:
The Sysmex PA-100 provided 
an optimal treatment recommendation in 218/278 cases (78.4%), against 162/278 (58.3%) of clinical decisions.

results.finding: QolorPhAST reported 100% species identification accuracy in a blinded study of 50 urine specimens from patients with suspected UTI.
results.detail: The excerpt gives 50 as the urine cohort size and leaves the denominators for the individual identification and susceptibility metrics unspecified.
results.quote: achieving 100% accuracy in species identification, an average categorical agreement of 91.81% and an average essential agreement of 86.4%

results.finding: QolorPhAST reported a 36-minute specimen-to-result time for identification and phenotypic susceptibility testing in a study of 50 urine specimens.
results.detail: Timing starts when the specimen enters the device. The excerpt gives no separate denominator for timed runs.
results.quote: with a turnaround time of 36 min from specimen introduction to result

results.finding: RDAP correctly detected and identified the organism in 15 of 16 clinical whole-blood specimens positive for a target.
results.detail: The single missed specimen contained 2 CFU/mL, below the prototype’s reported detection limit. Analytical validation used E. coli as the model organism.
results.quote: RDAP was able to detect and identify the correct species (as determined by standard lab procedure) in 15 out of 16 samples (93.8% accuracy).

results.finding: The Pattern prototype tested 166 lower respiratory specimens and achieved 96.8% on-panel pathogen identification sensitivity.
results.detail: Testing took place at Washington University, Cleveland Clinic, and Pattern. The reported 5–8 hours covers the cartridge assay after sample processing.
results.quote:
The Pattern assay 
achieved an overall sensitivity of 96.8% and an overall specificity of 98.1% (Table 3) across 1,660 comparisons (166 samples x 10 on-panel call groups).

results.finding: Cholkit detected all 19 culture-positive Vibrio cholerae O1 stools among 76 clinical specimens.
results.detail: Fresh stool specimens reached the laboratory 1–4 hours after collection. The evaluated prototype targeted V. cholerae O1.
results.quote: Out of 19 stools positive by culture, all 19 (100%) were positive by both Cholkit and Crystal VC assays, and 15 (79%) were positive by PCR (

results.finding: VITEK REVEAL GN AST achieved 95.0% agreement, both essential and categorical, for ceftazidime against P. aeruginosa across 101 clinical and challenge results.
results.detail: K260160 reanalyzed prior data to support adding P. aeruginosa to the ceftazidime indication.
results.quote:
The VITEK® REVEAL™ GN AST Assay demonstrated acceptable performance for P.  
aeruginosa/ceftazidime of 95.0% Essential Agreement and 95.0% Category Agreement with 
the reference method.

results.finding: QuickMIC GN averaged 3 h and 4 min to result in a comparison using 155 Gram-negative positive blood cultures.
results.detail: The study focused on routine workflows. Both US sites used BD Phoenix, and the study pooled their data for the comparator analysis. Table 4 gives an overall QuickMIC mean of 3 h and 5 min, one minute longer than the narrative reports.
results.quote:
QuickMIC time-to-result was on average 3 h and 4 min, 
compared to 9–19 h for the routine systems.

results.finding: FDA 510(k) K112000 cleared VITEK 2 AST-ST Penicillin. Among 350 S. pneumoniae isolates, categorical agreement at meningitis breakpoints was 97.7%.
results.detail: The meningitis analysis used 300 clinical and 50 challenge isolates with automated dilution. FDA deemed the error rates acceptable.
results.quote:
The submitted information in this premarket notification is complete and supports a 
substantial equivalence decision.

results.finding: FDA cleared the VersaTREK® MYCO PZA Kit under K052323 for M. tuberculosis pyrazinamide susceptibility testing from culture (96 isolates in the predicate comparison).
results.detail: Prescription use with the VersaTREK® Automated Microbial Detection System or ESP® Culture System II. The label requires confirmation of all resistant results by an alternate method.
results.quote:
The submitted information in this premarket notification is complete and supports 
a substantial equivalence decision

results.finding: PRATHAMASENSE reported direct detection of pathogens and AMR determinants within 90 minutes in a study that included 232 blood specimens.
results.detail: The 90-minute result applies to gene detection across the specimen types studied. The diagnostic comparisons used culture and qPCR, and the abstract provides no blood-specific concordance for organism–drug susceptibility or resistance.
results.quote: PRATHAMASENSE Genosensor delivers gene-specific detection of bacteria and fungi, including AMR determinants, directly from blood, tracheal fluid, and urine within 90 minutes - without a culture or PCR step.

results.finding: In 50 urine specimens from patients with suspected uncomplicated UTI, DropDx classified bacteria and assessed ciprofloxacin susceptibility in as little as 30 minutes.
results.detail: The reported time covered device operation after selection of refrigerated specimens. The study tested one antibiotic clinically and identified E. coli at species level, with broader categories for other bacteria.
results.quote: The corresponding refrigerated specimens were tested with DropDx right after selection and required less than 30 min of device operation.

results.finding: In gram-negative bloodstream infection (n = 448), 30-day in-hospital mortality was 3 percentage points higher with rapid testing using the reported rounded rates.
results.detail: The trial was powered for time to first antibiotic modification. The mortality comparison addresses one component of the required 30-day outcome.

results.finding: Among 204 patients evaluated for CNS infection, cerebrospinal fluid metagenomic sequencing alone identified 22% of confirmed infections.
results.detail: The diagnostic reference combined conventional testing with orthogonal testing of sequencing-positive findings, preventing unbiased sensitivity and specificity estimates. Resistance analyses were supplementary.
results.quote: Among these 58 infections, metagenomic NGS identified 13 (22%) that were not identified by clinical testing at the source hospital.

results.finding: Among 362 adults with complicated UTI, multiplex PCR-guided care increased 28-day complete clinical cure by 11.4 percentage points versus culture-guided care.
results.detail: The parent trial randomized 773 eligible patients, and the main cure analysis included 362. Timing excluded baseline empiric antibiotics given in the culture arm, so the reported interval concerns test-guided therapy.
results.quote:
Complete clinical cure (no baseline symptoms at EOS) occurred in 74.1% of PCR patients versus 62.7% of C&S patients (
p
= 0.020).

results.finding: For ICU hospital-acquired or ventilator-associated pneumonia (n=531), rapid PCR with optional prescribing guidance improved appropriate and proportionate antibiotic use by 21 percentage points.
results.detail: The 24-hour prescribing endpoint improved, but day-14 cure non-inferiority was not demonstrated. Enrolment began on 5 July 2019 and registration followed on 5 August 2019.
results.quote:
This randomised trial provides multi-centre evidence that rapid syn-
dromic PCR, delivered at the point-of care in the ICU improved anti-
biotic stewardship by 21% in absolute terms.

results.finding: Among 278 adults randomized for suspected gastroenteritis, point-of-care molecular testing returned results in a median of 1.7 hours.
results.detail: The primary endpoint was time in single-occupancy isolation. Antibiotic use increased, and the excerpt gives no evidence that the additional prescribing was appropriate. The screening count does not establish how many patients were eligible.
results.quote: The median (IQR) time to results was 1·7 h (1·5–2·0) for mPOCT and 44·7 h (21·2–66·1) for the control group (p<0·0001).

definition = "A service at the site of care identifies which organisms are causing a serious infection and reports which drugs are active against them in time to guide treatment. It distinguishes infection from incidental detection across clinical syndromes, including infections with several organisms and pathogens outside preset panels. A laboratory sequencing test for complicated urinary tract infection illustrates part of this capability: it identifies organisms in urine and predicts their susceptibility in about four hours from laboratory receipt.". Reason: The definition gains a clinical comparator that distinguishes a susceptibility prediction in one specimen type from the broader service.

goal.need = "At 131 US hospitals, 4,165 of 21,608 patients treated on the day of their first blood culture received no antibiotic active against their bloodstream isolate. Urine culture and susceptibility results can take two to four days. Earlier results can help clinicians replace an inactive drug or narrow treatment. A test for selected resistance genes can leave that choice unresolved. In gram-negative bloodstream infection, rapid testing brought antibiotic changes forward by a median of 14 hours without a demonstrated improvement in 30-day outcomes.". Reason: The current rationale omits how often initial treatment misses the infecting organism and what an earlier result lets a clinician change.

add statement by World Health Organization, 2020: "resistance testing/AST of prioritized bacterial pathogens". Reason: WHO’s 2020 profile explicitly pairs pathogen identification with susceptibility testing, which the existing WHO quotation does not establish.
add case "Respiratory infection". Reason: WHO names respiratory infection as a distinct syndrome for combined identification and susceptibility testing.
add case "Gastrointestinal infection". Reason: WHO includes gastrointestinal infection in the platform’s intended use, and blood or urine studies do not validate that use.

add milestone after None: "A diagnostic prototype demonstrates analytical performance on clinical or contrived specimens.". Reason: The existing milestones begin with a regulatory agreement threshold and omit the preceding demonstration of a working prototype.

edit m1: title = "A susceptibility assay reaches \u226590% essential and categorical agreement in gram-negative blood cultures."; criterion = "For positive blood cultures containing gram-negative rods, compare results with reference broth microdilution under K230675. Essential agreement requires minimum inhibitory concentrations within one twofold dilution of the reference. Categorical agreement requires the same susceptibility category. Both agreement rates must be \u226590%, false resistance \u22643% of reference-susceptible results and false susceptibility \u22642% of reference-resistant results, subject to the decision\u2019s specified adjustments and organism\u2013drug exceptions."; threshold_quote = "Performance was considered acceptable if the EA and CA were \u226590%, major error rate was \u22643%, and very major error rate was \u22642%."; threshold_ref = 7; refs = [7]. Reason: The criterion mixes FDA’s acceptance rule with the observed result for one drug–organism pair.

edit m2: title = "A sepsis blood test identifies 90% of bacterial isolates to species and 95% to genus."; criterion = "Using 1 mL of venous blood and blood culture as the reference, meet the TPP.S.II minimal diagnostic sensitivity target of 85\u201390% and identify 90% of isolates to species and 95% to genus. The minimal panel covers Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus spp., Staphylococcus aureus, Enterococcus spp., Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Salmonella."; set_by = "ICMR task force and Technical Advisory Group on AMR Diagnostics, Supplementary Table II, TPP.S.II, minimal targets."; threshold_quote = "Identifies 90 per cent of isolates to species level, 95 per cent to genus level"; threshold_ref = 6; refs = [6]. Reason: ICMR’s table supplies the missing identification threshold and confines it to the sepsis blood test.

add milestone after m2: "Two independent certified laboratories confirm a diagnostic prototype’s analytical claims.". Reason: The prize defines an independent analytical confirmation stage between developer testing and evaluation of patient outcomes.

edit m3: criterion = "FDA issues a 510(k) decision finding the susceptibility assay substantially equivalent for its labelled clinical use. The decision applies to the specimen types, organisms and conditions in the cleared indication."; set_by = "US Food and Drug Administration, 510(k) Premarket Notification database and decision summary."; threshold_quote = "Substantially Equivalent (SESE)"; threshold_ref = 8; refs = [8, 7]. Reason: The clearance criterion should identify the FDA decision a device must receive, while the date and indication of a particular clearance belong with its result.

add milestone after m4: "A district-hospital platform identifies priority bacteria and reports phenotypic susceptibility in 2–3 h.". Reason: WHO specifies a turnaround target for identification and phenotypic susceptibility together that neither of the individual ICMR test times establishes.

split m4 into "A sepsis test identifies blood pathogens within 4 hours at a price of ≤INR 500 per test." | "A sepsis test reports antimicrobial susceptibility in under 4 hours at ≤INR 2,000 per test.". Reason: ICMR permits identification and susceptibility tests to be developed independently and assigns them different time and price targets.

edit m5: title = "Rapid testing yields a better 30-day outcome with a lower 95% probability bound above 50%."; criterion = "In hospitalized patients with gram-negative bloodstream infection, randomize rapid phenotypic susceptibility testing plus standard testing against standard testing alone, with antimicrobial stewardship review in both groups. Rank 30-day outcomes from best to worst as alive without a deleterious event, alive with at least one such event, and death. Count a tie as one-half. The lower 95% confidence limit for the probability of a better outcome with rapid testing must exceed 50%."; threshold_quote = "Superiority was concluded if the lower limit of the 95% CI exceeded 50%."; threshold_ref = 2; refs = [10, 2]. Reason: The trial’s observed estimate belongs with its results, and the criterion needs to identify the randomized comparison to which the superiority bound applies.

edit m6: criterion = "In a first prospective evaluation at the intended care sites, meet the diagnostic, treatment-selection and patient-outcome endpoints registered before enrolment. Evaluate the complete service across the prespecified syndromes, including mixed infections and organisms outside preset panels. Compare causal attribution with clinical adjudication and susceptibility with reference testing. Assess whether results reach clinicians before the treatment decision, whether site cost and infrastructure limits are met, and whether patients benefit in a randomized comparison. Report coverage among all eligible patients."; set_by = "Technology Atlas proposes this integration milestone. No external body identified defines a test for the complete clinical workflow.". Reason: The integration criterion refers readers elsewhere for the workflow and ends with a summary of earlier results.
